tables.how: From the decisions analysis: every conditional-use, variance, large-project and historic-building record opened since 2015 whose status is approved, refused, withdrawn or cancelled (5,392). The district and neighborhood come from the parcel; the thirds are the City’s neighborhoods ranked on the Census 2020-24 survey and cut into three, as the case does. The tags are the analysis’s: a consultant when the firm or the applicant is on the Ethics Commission’s permit-consultant register; lobbied when the client name or the street address appears in a lobbyist’s report on planning; a donor firm when someone naming the firm as employer gave to a supervisor or mayoral committee in the two years before the decision. A firm is named only where the name reads as a company or body, or the firm is on a register; an applicant who may be a homeowner is never named.
tables.limits: A difference between areas is not proof of bias: places differ in zoning, lot size, building age and land price, and applicants withdraw for their own reasons. Firm names are matched after normalizing spelling, so a match is not proof that two records are one party. A lobbied address can be lobbied for a neighbor or an opponent, not only the applicant.

tables.how: From the votes analysis: each appeal number in the Board of Appeals minutes and case reports, with its outcome (denied, denied by default, granted with conditions, granted); 218 decided.
tables.limits: Several neighbors appealing one permit get one appeal number each. A holder or a person who appealed is named only where the name is a firm or body; a homeowner and a neighbor are never named. Members’ names are as the minutes print them.

tables.title: Every commission, Board of Appeals and Board of Supervisors decision placed in a census tract
tables.what: One decision on a project at an address: the Planning or Historic Preservation Commission, the Board of Appeals (a building permit appealed by someone other than the holder) or the Board of Supervisors (an appeal), with the census tract and whether it went against the project.

columns.t: Against the project, changed on review, or continued
Commissioners voting, as the minutes print them

tables.how: The votes analysis’s three selections: commission decisions placed by address (not legislation, legacy-business or landmark items) that were approved, approved with conditions, changed, disapproved or continued; Board of Appeals building-permit appeals by someone other than the holder; and Board of Supervisors appeals not brought by the applicant over a refusal.
tables.limits: The tract is an area, not the applicant; nothing is known or assumed about anyone who applied or objected. A continuance is often at the applicant’s request.

tables.title: Each lobbying contact about an address before a commission decision or a Board appeal at that address
tables.what: One contact a registered lobbyist reported, about a street address, with planning staff, a commissioner or a supervisor, in the two years before a decision at that address.

tables.how: The votes analysis’s rule: a contact’s issue text gives a street number and street that match the first two addresses of the decision, the contact is dated in the two years before, and for a commission decision the office is Planning or a planning commission; for a Board appeal the official is a supervisor who voted. 188 of 873 commission decisions at an address followed such a contact (120 with a commissioner who then voted), and 59 Board appeals.
tables.limits: Lobbying is registered; a contact is a report the lobbyist filed. A lobbyist may have worked for the project or against it, and the same number and street can be another building. A private client is not named.
